extracted.intended_audience: learned readers and students of theology/philosophy (early modern)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical theological discussion addressing the nature of the resurrection, eternal punishments, the doctrine of Purgatory, daemonology (apparitions/possession), and the legitimacy of related scriptural interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the Kingdom of God after Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Kingdome of God by Christ beginneth at the day of Judgment: That in that day, the Faithfull shall rise again, with glorious, and spirituall Bodies, and bee his Subjects in that his Kingdome, which shall be Eternall; That they shall neither marry, nor be given in marriage, nor eate and drink, as they did in their naturall bodies; but live for ever in their individuall persons, without the specificall eternity of generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the elect receive spiritual, immortal bodies at the Resurrection and will not continue earthly practices (marriage, eating). This distinguishes the elect's eternal life from mere perpetuation of bodily generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of the Reprobate after Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Reprobates also shall rise again, to receive punishments for their sins ... the bodies of the Reprobate ... shall also be glorious, or spirituall bodies, or that they shall bee as the Angels of God ... there is no place of Scripture to prove it; save onely these places concerning Eternall Torments; which may otherwise be interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues there is no scriptural proof that the reprobate receive the same spiritual/glorious bodies as the elect; instead they may rise to punishment. Emphasises need for careful scriptural interpretation rather than assuming parity of post‑resurrection states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Eternal Torments' and 'Eternal Fire'
rubrics_metrics.description: The texts that mention Eternall Fire, Eternal Torments, or the Word That Never Dieth, contradict not the Doctrine of a Second, and Everlasting Death, in the proper and naturall sense of the word Death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains that 'eternal' language about fire can be reconciled with a doctrine of a final Second Death: the fire may continue perpetually and there may always be wicked to be punished, but not necessarily that each individual suffers unending conscious torment. Notes possibility of punishment by succession rather than individual unending torment.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Reprobate may retain corruptible bodies and continue propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the wicked being left in the estate they were in after Adams sin, may at the Resurrection live as they did, marry, and give in marriage, and have grosse and corruptible bodies, as all mankind now have; and consequently may engender perpetually, after the Resurrection, as they did before: ... there is no place of Scripture to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Luke 20 (verses 34–36) and 1 Cor. 15 to argue the reprobate could be restored to an earthly-like immortality of kind (continued generation) but not the elect's personal immortality; distinction between immortality of persons vs immortality of kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Purgatory: lack of scriptural basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Onely of thus much, I see evident Scripture, to perswade men, that there is neither the word, nor the thing of Purgatory, neither in this, nor any other text; nor any thing that can prove a necessity of a place for the Soule without the Body ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys alleged proofs (David's fasting, other OT and NT texts) and finds them insufficient or strained; emphasizes that ceremonies of mourning and fasting are explicable by honour or private grief, not evidence of a third place for souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for judging scriptural proofs for doctrines (principle of contextual and literal alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where passages are alleged for Purgatory, many are rhetorical or metaphorical, and may be better interpreted as referring to the Day of Judgment, visions, or customary practices rather than a distinct interim place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages careful contextual reading (e.g., Matthew 12:32; 1 Cor. 15; Matthew 5 passages), comparison with prophetic and apocalyptic texts (Zachariah, Paul), and reluctance to force modern doctrinal conclusions onto ambiguous verses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Matthew 12:32 (words against Holy Ghost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whosoever speaketh a word against the Sonne of man, it shall be forgiven him; but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not bee forgiven him neither in this world, nor in the world to come: ... it is manifest, there are but three Worlds ... the World to come, and Purgatory, are inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers alternate readings: (a) a prophecy about the future unforgivingness of ecclesiastical authorities acting by the Holy Ghost; (b) possible (but paradoxical) allowance for repentance after the Resurrection. Uses the three-world framework to reject equating 'world to come' with Purgatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1 Corinthians 3: 'saved, but as through fire'—day of judgment as refining fire
rubrics_metrics.description: They themselves shall be saved; but as through Fire: ... an allusion to Zach. 13.9 and the final Day of Judgment, where the Elect are refined and erroneous doctrines sindged off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets the apostolic 'fire' as the universal refining fire at Christ's coming (refining doctrines and purging error), not as proof of a current purgatorial fire tormenting incorporeal souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding 'Baptism for the dead' (1 Cor 15) and prayers for the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: Of many interpretations ... by Baptisme is meant (metaphorically) a Baptisme of Penance ... or there was a custome by receiving Baptisme for the dead ... and then the forgivenesse of sins in the world to come, has no need of a Purgatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents competing explanations (metaphorical baptism of penance; proxy baptism custom) and concludes neither yields decisive support for Purgatory; allows that prayers for the dead may be useful if God, by such prayers or providence, converts those who had not heard the Gospel before the Resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew 5:25 ('pay the uttermost farthing') allegory against Purgatory inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree with thine Adversary quickly ... thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou has paid the uttermost farthing. ... the Offender is the Sinner; both the Adversary and the Judge is God; the Way is this Life; the Prison is the Grave ... the sinner shall not rise again to life eternall, but to a second Death, till he have paid the utmost farthing, or Christ pay it for him by his Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reads the passage as allegorical about final judgment and Christ's atonement rather than evidence for an intermediate purgatorial state where temporary punishments are endured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew 5:22 (angry/insults) not evidence for graded postmortem courts
rubrics_metrics.description: From which words he inferreth three sorts of Sins, and three sorts of Punishments; and that none of those sins, but the last, shall be punished with hell fire; and consequently, that after this life, there is punishment of lesser sins in Purgatory. Of which inference, there is no colour ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the passage is aimed at intensifying the Law (inward dispositions equal murder) and not at establishing multiple postmortem courts or tiers of punishment; interpretation must consider surrounding context and Jesus' interpretive aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luke 16:9 ('make friends of unrighteous mammon') not proof for invocation of saints
rubrics_metrics.description: He alledges to prove Invocation of Saints departed. But the sense is plain, That we should make friends with our Riches, of the Poore, and thereby obtain their Prayers whilest they live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-interpretation: passage concerns almsgiving to the poor to secure prayers/benefits during life, not postmortem invocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luke 23:42 (thief's plea) — Christ's forgiveness as case not proof of postmortem remission
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord remember me when thou commest into thy Kingdome: Therefore, saith hee, there is Remission of sins after this life. But the consequence is not good. Our Saviour then forgave him; and at his comming againe in Glory, will remember to raise him againe to Life Eternall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats the thief's pardon as immediate forgiveness by Christ and future resurrection, not evidence for a system of purgatorial remission after death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts 2:24 ('loosed the pains of death') not descent into Purgatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts 2.24 where St. Peter saith of Christ, 'that God had raised him up, and loosed the Paines of Death, because it was not possible he should be holden of it;' Which hee interprets to bee a descent of Christ into Purgatory ... whereas it is manifest, that it was Christ that was loosed; it was hee that could not bee holden of Death, or the Grave; and not the Souls in Purgatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read as Christ's victory over death rather than a narrative of descending into and liberating souls from a purgatorial place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and nature of apparitions (daemonology) as psychological/physiological phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression made on the organs of Sight ... produceth in living Creatures ... an Imagination of the Object, from whence the Impression proceedeth; which Imagination is called Sight ... the motion made by this pressure, continuing after the object which caused it is removed, is that we call Imagination, and Memory, and (in sleep ... ) a Dream ... this is that we call Daemons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains apparitions and so‑called 'daemons' as internal impressions, imaginations, or memories produced by sensory organs and neural motions (e.g., afterimages, dreams, pressure on the eye), not necessarily independent incorporeal beings. Encourages naturalistic explanation of visions.

rubrics_metrics.name: How ancients misattributed brain phantasms to external spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: This nature of Sight having never been discovered by the ancient pretenders ... it was hard for men to conceive of those Images in the Fancy ... otherwise, than of things really without us ... And by that means have feared them, as things of an unknown, that is, of an unlimited power to doe them good, or harme; and consequently, given occasion to the Governours of the Heathen Common-wealths to regulate ... DAEMONOLOGY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical explanation: cultural and political institutions exploited fear of visions by constructing daemonologies, assigning divine or demonic agencies to internal phenomena; interpret such beliefs as social constructs rather than literal accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural language about 'spirits' often denotes visions or internal motions, not incorporeal spectres
rubrics_metrics.description: Where our Saviour speaketh to the Devill, and commandeth him to go out of a man, if by the Devill, be meant a Disease, as Phrenesy, or Lunacy, or a corporeal Spirit, is not the speech improper? ... the addressing of our Saviours command to the Madnesse, or Lunacy he cureth, is no more improper, then was his rebuking of the Fever, or of the Wind, and Sea; ... those speeches are not improper, because they signifie the power of Gods Word: no more therefore is it improper, to command Madnesse, or Lunacy ... to depart out of a mans body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates reading many biblical 'spirit' and 'devil' passages as rhetorical or therapeutic language addressing disorders or visions, rather than literal references to incorporeal beings possessing bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptures do not teach incorporeal spirits inhabiting bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: I find in Scripture that there be Angels, and Spirits, good and evill; but not that they are Incorporeall, as are the Apparitions men see in the Dark, or in a Dream, or Vision ... And I find that there are Spirits Corporeal, (though subtile and Invisible;) but not that any mans body was possessed, or inhabited by them;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims biblical evidence supports corporeal (though subtle) spirits and spiritual bodies at resurrection, not immaterial, independent spectres inhabiting human bodies; urges caution in reading 'possession' narratives as literal invasions by immaterial beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary gifts (exorcisms, miracles) diminished after primitive church
rubrics_metrics.description: Neverthelesse, the contrary Doctrine, namely, that there be Incorporeall Spirits, hath hitherto so prevailed in the Church, that the use of Exorcisme ... is thereupon built; ... That there were many Daemoniaques in the Primitive Church, and few Mad-men, and other such singular diseases; whereas in these times we hear of, and see many Mad-men, and few Daemoniaques, proceeds not from the change of Nature; but of Names. ... those extraordinary gifts were given to the Church, for no longer a time, than men trusted wholly to Christ ... and consequently, that when they sought Authority, and Riches, and trusted to their own Subtilty for a Kingdome of this world, these supernaturall gifts of God were again taken from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains decline of miraculous gifts as historically contingent — temporary charisms given in early church when believers wholly trusted Christ; later social changes (seeking authority, wealth) led to their diminution; cautions against expecting the same signs today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship of images as Pagan relic and idolatry defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Another relique of Gentilisme, is the Worship of Images ... it was the generall Religion of the Gentiles, to worship for Gods, those Apparences that remain in the Brain ... this is the reason why St. Paul says, 'Wee know that an Idol is Nothing:' Not that he thought that an Image of Metall, Stone, or Wood, was nothing; but that the thing which they honored, or feared in the Image, and held for a God, was a meer Figment ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that idolatry consists in venerating mental representations as if they were real independent gods; recommends understanding images as representations produced by the brain, and condemns divine honour paid to such figments as rebellion against the true God.
